clue.text: Stop press news: half-century at a cricket match

parts.note: L is the Roman numeral for fifty
a Test is an international cricket match

explanation.surface: A late newspaper bulletin reporting a batsman's fifty in a cricket match.
explanation.walkthrough: A Test is a top-level international cricket match, lasting up to five days.
explanation.definitionFit: Stop press items are the most recent reports, added after a paper has gone to press.

clue.text: See 14
Artist to draw explorer

parts.note: to draw a game is to tie it
Marco Polo, the Venetian traveller to China

explanation.surface: A painter is asked to sketch a famous explorer.
explanation.walkthrough: 'draw' looks like the artist's verb but means finishing level in a contest.
explanation.definitionFit: Giovanni Battista Tiepolo was an eighteenth-century Venetian painter famous for ceiling frescoes.

clue.text: Superficial variety embraced by diocesan president

indicators.note: something embraced is held inside the arms of another, so one word sits within another

parts.note: a see is a bishop's diocese
a kind is a sort or variety
P is the abbreviation for president

explanation.surface: Some type of thing is hugged by the man presiding over a diocese.
explanation.walkthrough: A see is the seat or district of a bishop, a crossword favourite for diocese.
explanation.definitionFit: Something only skin-deep goes no further than the surface, so it is shallow or superficial.

clue.text: Unemployed having lots of money

parts.note: idle means out of work
rich means wealthy

explanation.surface: A description of people who do no work yet are wealthy.
explanation.walkthrough: The two halves give the two words, and the whole clue describes the people they name.
explanation.definitionFit: The idle rich are wealthy people who need not work for a living, living off inherited wealth.

clue.text: Hell bent? Far from it!

definitions.note: in context: far from being bent on something

parts.note: Dis is the classical underworld, Hell
bent on something means inclined towards it

explanation.surface: Someone asked whether they are hell-bent on something replies that they are not at all.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Hell bent' reads as one idiom, but Hell and bent are separate pieces; 'Far from it!' says the person is not bent at all.
explanation.definitionFit: To be disinclined is to be reluctant, the very opposite of being determined or hell-bent on a course.

clue.text: End of life for Riley, in a weird sort of way

definitions.text: in a weird sort of way

indicators.note: the end of a word is its final letter, so only that is kept

parts.note: the final letter only

indicators.note: something weird is strange and twisted out of its normal shape, so the name is rearranged

parts.note: the name taken as written, to be rearranged

explanation.surface: A man called Riley meets his end in some strange fashion.
explanation.walkthrough: 'The life of Riley' is the comfortable life; here the end of life is just its last letter. 'weird' serves both as the rearranging word and in the definition.
explanation.definitionFit: Eerily means strangely or uncannily, in a manner that is unsettling or spooky.

clue.text: The other way for most of Shakespeare?

definitions.meaning: first meaning: the opposite, the reverse direction
second meaning, split into two words: the form most of his plays are written in

explanation.walkthrough: Split as IN VERSE, the answer describes Shakespeare's plays, which are mostly written in blank verse.
explanation.definitionFit: The inverse of something is its opposite or reversal, the other way round from the original.

clue.text: The kinkajou has to sharpen its hearing by climbing in

indicators.note: the little word is placed in, between the other two pieces

parts.note: to hone is to sharpen a blade
an ear is the faculty of hearing

indicators.note: in a down clue climbing means going upwards, so the little word reads from bottom to top

parts.note: taken as written

explanation.surface: A small rainforest animal must sharpen its hearing while it clambers up a tree.
explanation.walkthrough: 'by' looks like a mere preposition in the surface, but it is a piece of the answer in its own right.
explanation.definitionFit: The kinkajou is a tree-dwelling South American mammal commonly called the honey bear for its taste for honey.

clue.text: Quote compiler the wrong way — it makes one sick

indicators.note: going the wrong way means travelling backwards, so the words are read from right to left

parts.note: to cite is to quote
the compiler is the setter, who calls himself me

explanation.surface: Someone complains that quoting the puzzle-setter badly turns the stomach.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Quote compiler' is read as an instruction, CITE ME, and the whole is then reversed. The compiler is the crossword setter.
explanation.definitionFit: An emetic is a substance taken to induce vomiting, so it makes the person who takes it sick.

clue.text: See 20
Little one for the upper house? Tory fell around convulsed

definitions.text: Little one for the upper house?

indicators.note: a convulsed body is thrown into violent spasms, so the letters are thrown about

parts.note: the fodder taken as written

explanation.surface: A Conservative politician collapses in a fit while debating the House of Lords.
explanation.walkthrough: The definition plays on the title Little Lord Fauntleroy: a little lord is one destined for the House of Lords, the upper house.
explanation.definitionFit: Little Lord Fauntleroy is the young heir to an earldom in Frances Hodgson Burnett's novel, a junior peer.

clue.text: Performance by First Lady in a ring, not shortened

parts.note: taken as written

indicators.note: the lady is placed in the middle of the other word

parts.note: a bell's ring is a chime
Eve was the first woman in Genesis

indicators.note: the word loses its heart and keeps only its outside letters

parts.note: only the first and last letters of the word

explanation.surface: The President's wife gives a performance in a boxing ring, uncut.
explanation.walkthrough: 'not shortened' reads as 'in full', but the first word is a piece and the second an instruction on it. First Lady is Eve, not a president's wife.
explanation.definitionFit: An achievement is something accomplished, a performance or feat carried out successfully.

clue.text: Make love at opening of door in cave

parts.note: to woo is to court, an old sense of making love
the keyhole is an opening in a door

explanation.surface: A couple make love at the entrance to a cave.
explanation.walkthrough: Wookey Hole is a show cave in the Mendip Hills of Somerset, England. 'Make love' is meant in the old sense of courting.
explanation.definitionFit: Wookey Hole is a well-known limestone cave system in Somerset, so it is an example of a cave.

clue.text: Two rare accessions form the bottom line, as it were

definitions.text: the bottom line, as it were

indicators.note: to form is to shape something, so these letters are shaped into a new arrangement

parts.note: the fodder taken as written

explanation.surface: Two unusual additions to a library collection make up the final total in its accounts.
explanation.walkthrough: 'bottom line' usually means the final figure; 'as it were' signals reading it as the lowest possible outcome.
explanation.definitionFit: A worst-case scenario is the most pessimistic outcome imaginable, the lowest point things could reach.

clue.text: "He trusts" is written on his grave

parts.note: taken as written
to rely on someone is to trust them

explanation.surface: An epitaph declaring a man's faith is carved on his tombstone.
explanation.walkthrough: HE RELIES is respaced as HERE LIES, the traditional opening of an epitaph.
explanation.definitionFit: The words open countless epitaphs, so they are what is commonly carved on a tombstone.

clue.text: See 13
People move fast

definitions.meaning: first meaning: a people or ethnic group
second meaning: to rush or hurry

explanation.walkthrough: The surface reads as an order to a crowd to hurry; the two parts are separate meanings.
explanation.definitionFit: A race can be a nation or people sharing descent, and to race is to go at speed.

clue.text: Wreath for the little man?

parts.note: a chap is a man
-let is a suffix making things little, as in piglet

explanation.surface: A garland offered to a small fellow.
explanation.walkthrough: 'little man' reads as a short person, but little is the diminutive ending added after the man.
explanation.definitionFit: A chaplet is a garland or wreath worn on the head, a crown of flowers or leaves.

clue.text: Vulgar parlance? The same, with gap left out

definitions.meaning: surface reading: coarse or rude talk

definitions.text: The same, with gap left out
definitions.meaning: setter's reading: vulgar in its old sense of common, the everyday tongue of ordinary people; the rest seems to describe that same speech with its gaps, its dropped letters, elided

explanation.surface: Someone asks whether crude language is just ordinary speech with bits missing.
explanation.walkthrough: Vulgar here is the Latin sense of 'of the common people', not 'rude'. The second half is obscure and may hint that gap is a lacuna, whose letters the answer contains.
explanation.definitionFit: The vernacular is the everyday language of ordinary people, which is what vulgar originally meant.

clue.text: Hide the king outside

indicators.note: the royal name stands outside, wrapped around the other word

parts.note: King Lear of Shakespeare's tragedy
taken as written

explanation.surface: An order to conceal the monarch out of doors.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Hide' looks like a verb but is the noun, an animal's skin: LEA(THE)R.
explanation.definitionFit: Leather is tanned animal skin, and a hide is the skin of a large animal.

clue.text: Very white snake with excretions died a split second before this moment

parts.note: the asp is an Egyptian snake
urea is a compound excreted in urine; plural here
d. is the abbreviation for died
riven means split apart
s is the abbreviation for second
now is this moment

explanation.surface: A pale snake with its waste products dies in an instant just before now.
explanation.walkthrough: 'a split second' looks like one phrase, but split and second are separate pieces.
explanation.definitionFit: Freshly driven snow is the proverbial image of spotless whiteness and purity, so the simile means very white.

clue.text: Mystical Pole in ecstasy has indefinite number of teeth

indicators.note: the pole is placed in the state of rapture

parts.note: a trance is a state of rapture
S for the South Pole
n stands for an unspecified number in maths
dental means relating to teeth

explanation.surface: A Polish man in rapture has an unknown number of teeth.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Pole' looks like a Polish person but is a compass pole: TRAN(S)CE + N + DENTAL.
explanation.definitionFit: Transcendental describes the spiritual or mystical, beyond ordinary experience, as in transcendental meditation.

clue.text: See 20
Everyone on leave, without energy, on the Western front?

definitions.note: completes the title All Quiet on the Western Front

parts.note: all means everyone

indicators.note: without in its old sense of outside, so one word goes around the letter

parts.note: to quit is to leave
E is the symbol for energy

explanation.surface: All the soldiers in a First World War trench go on leave, too exhausted to fight.
explanation.walkthrough: 'without' looks like minus but means outside: QUI(E)T. The answer is the start of the title of Remarque's war novel.
explanation.definitionFit: The novel's title says there is no fighting, so the words describe the calm on that front.

clue.text: Deprived person or phantom cat gone missing

parts.note: taken as written

indicators.note: something gone missing is no longer there, so these letters are taken away

parts.note: taken as written
a tom is a male cat

explanation.surface: A deprived person, or perhaps a ghostly cat, has vanished.
explanation.walkthrough: The answer is in plain view across 'or phantom'; the cat is the male one, a tom, which is what goes missing.
explanation.definitionFit: An orphan is a child deprived of parents, so a person bereft of mother and father.

clue.text: Request for opposing bridge players to find agreement

parts.note: East and North sit at adjacent sides, opponents in bridge
a treaty is a formal agreement

explanation.surface: A plea for two rival card players to reach a deal.
explanation.walkthrough: Bridge players are named by compass points; East and North are on opposing sides.
explanation.definitionFit: An entreaty is an earnest plea or appeal, a request made urgently to someone.

clue.text: Don't buy his books!

parts.note: surface reading: a call to boycott some author's work; setter's reading: the instruction to get a book from the library instead, and the surname of George, the nineteenth-century English author of Lavengro and The Bible in Spain

explanation.surface: A call to boycott some author's work.
explanation.walkthrough: The word is both the advice (get it on loan rather than buy) and the author whose books are meant.
explanation.definitionFit: To borrow is to take something on loan instead of purchasing it; George Borrow was a Victorian travel writer.
